description:
We are a school robotics team from Escola Integrada Educativa in Sumaré, São Paulo, Brazil, participating in NASA Space Apps through the Campinas event. Our interest in robotics, science, and space exploration inspired us to create Marsway.

Through this project, we combined programming, teamwork, and creativity to make Mars exploration more accessible, connecting scientific evidence with exploration planning and interactive learning.
summary:
Marsway is an interactive exploration planner that helps astronauts decide where to explore next on Mars. It brings together NASA imagery, scientific source evidence, and destination comparisons in one accessible workspace.

Users can place a simulated base, adjust their study interests, compare destinations by preference-based scores and distance, inspect supporting evidence, and organize a round-trip plan. Missing terrain information remains visible, and travel lines represent distance estimates rather than verified traversable routes. A rover arcade game lets users explore their planned destinations through fictional terrain, connecting planning with an engaging learning experience.

Marsway addresses the challenge of turning planetary data into understandable exploration decisions. Instead of presenting imagery alone, it connects places, sources, priorities, and planning while making uncertainty explicit.

This matters because informed exploration depends on understanding both what the evidence supports and what remains unknown. Marsway makes Mars data more approachable while keeping users in control of their decisions.
details:
Marsway is a browser-based exploration planner that helps astronauts decide where to explore next on Mars. It connects NASA imagery, published scientific evidence, destination comparisons, and simulated round-trip planning in one workspace.

Users begin by setting a simulated base. They can discover named Martian features, adjust study interests, and compare destinations using transparent preference-based scores and distance estimates.

An evidence inspector connects destinations to source records, imagery, and available geological context while identifying missing information.

After choosing destinations, users can organize their visit order and return to base. Optional speed, work-time, and reserve assumptions support preliminary time estimates. Plans can be saved locally, exported, imported, and printed without an account.

Marsway also includes a pilotable rover arcade game. Users can drive a schematic version of their plan, follow destination checkpoints, scan them, and return home. Its fictional terrain and compressed distances are clearly distinguished from scientific maps and real rover capabilities.

We developed Marsway using React, TypeScript, Vite, and CesiumJS, with a Canvas-based rover game and Playwright browser tests. Scientific resources include NASA mission imagery and observations, an IAU/USGS feature catalogue, and geological and terrain context products. Sources and limitations are documented within the application.

The project’s creative contribution is connecting evidence-based exploration planning with an interactive learning experience. It makes planetary information more approachable while preserving important uncertainties: scores reflect user preferences, terrain suitability remains unknown, and trip lines estimate distance rather than verified traversable routes.

Marsway supports informed exploration by helping users understand both what available evidence shows and what still needs investigation.
